beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent runs our own policies against the system and sorts which rules it can check from files and which it can't. I can see the report myself.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell it which data and customers matter, and it shapes the check around that. Reasonable.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: A long interview with the agent. It's useful if the questions are good, and I can't tell that from the page.

beats.trigger: Make the rules sound like your company's policy, not a generic GDPR template.
beats.got: Checking the output against our own policy is my job. It won't do that by itself.

beats.trigger: Ask the agent to install the authored source.
beats.got: Setup steps for saving the file. Skippable.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: This doesn't replace our security function. It adds an agent-specific layer on top of it. That is the answer to the first thing I'd ask.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: The saved check shows up as a command. That's how I know it is installed.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit gives me three lists: what complies, what violates, and what it can't tell. It says openly when it doesn't know, and I can open the report and verify it.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The agent ranks the risks in my system and explains each one. The line about feelings is the kind of thing I'd expect on a transformation slide.

beats.trigger: Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.
beats.got: When the agent can't settle a question, I take the report to legal or security and ask them one narrow question. That's how I'd actually work.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: We handled one risk in this session. A production agent needs every risk handled. Straight and candid.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the audit session and adds one to five rules to the root instructions file for future sessions.
beats.got: The agent writes what it learned into a rules file so the next session starts with it. I'd want to read those rules before trusting them.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Skills can be handed to a colleague, but it's not a deployed service and nobody owns it by default.

beats.trigger: Remember that success with AI is everyone's responsibility.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework with a mild guilt trip. I'll see if I do it.

beats.trigger: Read Mata v. Avianca (2023) and Deloitte Australia / DEWR report (2025) in the lecture.
beats.got: Two real cases with names and years, and I can look them up myself.

take_homes: Agent security needs its own check on top of our normal controls. The risk is that it can be talked into things by documents it reads.
The cheapest mitigation is giving it less access, and that costs a feature. Someone senior signs for what's left over.
The agent's check says which rules it can't judge. That's when I take the specific question to legal or security.

monday.move: Ask our security lead one question: has anyone checked what the AI tools already in use here can read and change?
monday.when: If it comes up at this week's steering group; otherwise it waits
monday.stop_condition: They say there is a policy and someone owns it
monday.blocker: A calendar full of the last programme's steering groups, and I don't use Claude Code myself

misconception.why: The check ran on the system and reported "I can't tell" for some rules, which I could open and verify. The premise that agent risk is new and not covered by old controls is also fair. I still think the adoption talk is hype, but waiting is not obviously the safe move any more.

one_line: About a third of it is the usual 'rapidly evolving landscape' filler, but the rest was honest: it costs a feature, here's what it can't tell you, and here's what separates a prototype from production.
